1.pericope_label: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches ... the rich and poor meet together: the Lord is the maker of them all ... a prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself ... by humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, and honour, and life
debates: In what sense rich and poor meet: Gill offers a hostile meeting, a mutual dependence, and an exchange of places; Clarke works it out economically; Keil and Delitzsch make the meeting itself a divine ordinance and a school of virtue; Henry takes it of the bar of justice and the throne of grace.

How the fourth verse construes: Ellicott and Gill report the rendering that makes the fear of the Lord the reward of humility, which Keil and Delitzsch say the old interpreters took, while others read two virtues joined without a connective and Henry keeps the received sense.
outliers: Gill and Clarke both note that the word good is supplied by the old versions and absent from the text.
themes: A name worth more than riches
Rich and poor made by one hand
Foresight and the refusal of warning

5.pericope_label: Thorns and snares are in the way of the froward ... train up a child in the way he should go ... the rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender ... he that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity
debates: What the way he should go means: Keil and Delitzsch reject the calling, the course of life and the individual temperament, and settle on the nature of childhood as such; Clarke reads an initiation at the opening of the path and a dedication to God; Henry contrasts the way the child would go with the way he should.
Whether the rule of the rich is usurpation or ordinance: Gill has them usurp a dominion and use it rigorously, Clarke says the arrangement is in the order of God and may be a blessing to both.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch note that the group closing at the eighth verse ends the first collection of these proverbs, and closes, like the one before it, with a saying about poor and rich.
Henry allows the exception, that many have left the way they were trained in, Solomon among them, and rests on the parents having done their duty.
Clarke quotes a Latin poet on the odour a new jar retains from its first wine, meeting Henry’s image of the vessel keeping the savour it was first seasoned with.
themes: A crooked way with thorns in it
Instruction fitted to the child
Power and debt as the course of the world

9.pericope_label: He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed ... cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out ... he that loveth pureness of heart, for the grace of his lips the king shall be his friend ... the eyes of the Lord preserve knowledge
debates: How the eleventh verse construes: Keil and Delitzsch rule out three readings, that a man loves with a pure heart, that gracious lips follow from loving purity, and that he loves grace on his own lips, and prefer the sense that a true heart and amiable speech win the king’s friendship.

Which king is meant: Henry reports that some understand the King of kings and cites the officer styled the king’s friend at the old courts; Clarke takes the heavenly sense outright while giving a reason for the earthly one.

What preserving knowledge means: Keil and Delitzsch argue that knowledge stands by metonymy for men of knowledge, since God’s eyes cannot keep themselves by a rule; Gill and Clarke instance the preservation of the Scriptures.
outliers: Gill rejects the reading that makes the scorner the corrupt nature within, since that can be weakened but not cast out.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the Greek adds a couplet at the ninth verse which the Hebrew does not have.
themes: The eye that seeks out want
The scorner and the peace of a society
Purity and speech that win a king

13.pericope_label: The slothful man saith, There is a lion without ... the mouth of strange women is a deep pit ... foolishness is bound in the heart of a child ... he that oppresseth the poor to increase his riches
debates: What the folly bound in a child’s heart is: Gill and Henry take original corruption, Keil and Delitzsch a childish pleasure in stupid tricks and silly sport, Ellicott self-will that has to be taught to yield.

How the sixteenth verse construes: Keil and Delitzsch canvass several readings, including one referring the two participles to two classes of men, and object that the intended antithesis then fails; Ellicott makes the oppressor thereby a giver to the rich, obliged to disgorge his prey to someone stronger.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch note that the strong word for murder is chosen to make the sluggard’s pretence hyperbolical, and that he states it flatly, without a perhaps or a lest.
Clarke sets the descent in Virgil beside the deep pit, where the way down is smooth but the return is the long unconquerable pain.
themes: Excuses invented by sloth
A pit that few climb out of
Correction and the folly it drives out

17.pericope_label: Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise ... have not I written to thee excellent things in counsels and knowledge, that I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth
debates: What the word rendered excellent things means: Clarke and Gill both canvass the reading that makes it a numeral, listing the three books of Solomon, the three divisions of the canon, three sciences and the three senses of Scripture, and both settle on excellent or princely things; Gill objects that part of the canon did not then exist.

Who wrote the section beginning here: Keil and Delitzsch make these verses a prologue to an appendix written after the Solomonic collection; Ellicott infers from the plural that the proverbs are by others than Solomon; Henry marks only a change of manner.
outliers: Ellicott hears in the emphatic to thee, even to thee that a message general in form is addressed to each soul; Henry hears instead a warning that what is made known today may before tomorrow be hidden.
Clarke lays the five verses out as a numbered scheme rather than as proverbs.
themes: A new division and a direct address
Words kept in the heart and fitted on the lips
Truth learnt in order to be taught

22.pericope_label: Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate ... make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul
debates: How the particle in the first clause works: Gill offers both because he is poor and though he is poor, the one making the poverty the reason for the robbery and the other refusing it as an inducement.
outliers: Henry notices the anticlimax, that after so solemn a preface the first of the words of the wise is a plain and common caution.
Ellicott and Clarke note that the gate was the place of business and of judgment, courts being held at city gates; Ellicott points to a government still named from a gate.
Keil and Delitzsch note that these verses fall into quatrains, and that the angry man is named a master of anger as a covetous man is a master of appetite.
themes: Robbery made worse by the victim’s helplessness
God taking the place of counsel and judge
Company that teaches its own temper

26.pericope_label: Be not thou one of them that strike hands ... remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set. Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings
debates: How far the landmark applies to religion: Gill allows doctrines settled by Christ and the apostles to be called ancient landmarks but refuses the title to those of the fathers who followed, as fallible men; Clarke forbids new dogmas and rites not laid down in Scripture, yet insists that calling a church back to doctrines it has lost is not removing a landmark.

How to grade the offence of suretiship: Gill calls it weakness to be bound when unable to pay and wickedness to be bound knowing one cannot answer; Henry distinguishes the man disabled by providence, who should be pitied, from the man who picks his neighbour’s pocket.
outliers: Ellicott notes that a garment taken in pledge had to be returned before sundown for the poor man to sleep in, and that the provision was evidently evaded.
Clarke quotes a Latin poet on the god who presided over boundaries, with both owners bringing garlands and libations and the neighbourhood keeping a festival; Gill reports the same deity briefly.
Keil and Delitzsch note a variant reading taken by one rabbi of those brought up out of the land of bondage and by another of the poor.
themes: Suretyship and the bed taken in pledge
Boundaries made sacred by age
Diligence rare enough to be rewarded
